summary: One of a series of surveys by David Smallberg checking which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP. This edition tested hosts in December 1982 and January 1983. Replaced by RFC 836.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on the door of every computer on the list to see which ones answered. This is the result for one week.

subtitle: December 1982 snapshot of TCP service adoption across early Internet hosts.

tldr.problem: In the early 1980s, it was unclear which computers on the emerging Internet could accept connections for important services like Telnet, FTP and email.
tldr.mechanism: A researcher at Stanford tested connectivity to every host in the NIC hostname table, checking whether they responded to Telnet, FTP, and SMTP connections.
tldr.outcome: The survey found that 61 hosts accepted Telnet, 43 accepted FTP, and 44 accepted SMTP, revealing how unevenly TCP services were deployed in December 1982. This edition was replaced by RFC 836 with updated data a month later.

today: RFC 836 published an updated survey one month later with January 1983 data, superceding these December results.

sections.title: A Snapshot of TCP Adoption
sections.content:
RFC 835 is a survey by David Smallberg documenting which Internet hosts could accept connections for Telnet (remote login), FTP (file transfer), and SMTP (email) using the newly deployed TCP protocol in December 1982. The survey tested 314 hosts drawn from the NIC hostname table.

The data was gathered from December 28 to 29, 1982, with a follow-up test on December 29. Dead, refused, and unreachable hosts were retried to ensure accuracy.
sections.eli5: Someone went through the list of all known computers and tried to reach each one on three different services to see which ones worked.

sections.title: Survey Methodology
sections.content:
For each service, hosts were classified based on the NIC hostname table claims: t for TCP/Telnet capability, f for TCP/FTP, and s for TCP/SMTP. When tested, each host received one of six responses: no service, refused, unreachable, dead, accepted, or for FTP, accepted with anonymous guest login.

The RFC presents results in two formats: summary tables showing counts by service, and a detailed alphabetical list of every host and its results for each service.
sections.eli5: Each computer was labeled with what it claimed to do, then the survey tried to connect and recorded whether it worked, was refused, or was unreachable.

sections.title: Key Findings
sections.content:
Of 314 hosts tested, adoption was uneven: 61 accepted Telnet (against 130 that claimed capability), 43 accepted FTP (of 107 claiming it), and 44 accepted SMTP (of 96 claiming it). Many hosts were dead or unreachable, and about 30 percent of hosts claiming services refused connections. The survey also found that 26 hosts that claimed only generic TCP support (not specific services) did accept connections to all three services.

This revealed a gap between claimed capabilities and actual deployment: many systems listed in the hostname table were either offline, unreachable from the test site, or had not yet implemented promised services.
sections.eli5: Many computers said they could do these things, but only about a third of them actually answered when contacted. Some were broken or not connected.

sections.title: Survey Data Details
sections.content:
The RFC includes a complete alphabetical listing of all 314 hosts, showing each host's IP address, claimed capabilities, and connection results for Telnet, FTP, and SMTP. The data reveals patterns: systems at major institutions like BBN, Carnegie Mellon, Stanford, and UCLA had working TCP services, while many smaller or less-connected hosts had none.

The survey found that facilities with FTP access sometimes offered anonymous guest access (shown as accepted+ in the data), allowing password-less file downloads. These special-case hosts were markers of public-access file services.
sections.eli5: The RFC lists every computer tested and shows which services answered. You could see which big organizations had working TCP and which ones didn't.
